# Closing Look - 8/28/26

### Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivered his first Jackson Hole keynote as chair, striking a hawkish tone that pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher and pressured stocks into the close.

[![Frank Cappelleri's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9lPT!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fda78e20e-2e56-4a13-8edd-9197b778042e_3153x3153.jpeg)](https://substack.com/@cappnotes)

# Summary

The S&P 500, Nasdaq, and Russell 2000 all finished lower, while the Dow was roughly flat, though all four indices still closed out the week with gains.

Nvidia ( **NVDA**) fell despite a blowout quarterly beat, as the broader chip complex failed to extend Thursday’s rally.

PayPal ( **PYPL**) was the session’s biggest single-stock story, tumbling after a reported buyout consortium abandoned its roughly $50 billion takeover pursuit.

Gold logged an outsized drop as the hawkish Fed repricing lifted real yields, and a wave of post-earnings reactions across retail, fintech, and semiconductors kept the tape volatile beneath a quiet headline number.

## Major Indices & Breadth

- 🔴 **Dow Jones** dipped **-0.02%** to **53,559.34**, essentially flat as gains in a handful of mega-cap and consumer names offset losses across chips and industrials.

- 🔴 **S&P 500** closed at **7,711.48**, **-0.25%**, cooling off after the post-Nvidia rally as Fed Chair Warsh’s hawkish tone weighed into the close — the index still finished the week higher.

- 🔴 **Nasdaq Composite** fell **-0.52%** to **26,402.42**, the session’s biggest percentage decliner among the majors as chipmakers gave back some of Thursday’s surge.

- 🔴 **Russell 2000** underperformed, falling **-1.30%** to **2,975.13** as small-caps proved most sensitive to the rate-hike repricing.

- 🔴 Breadth was negative, with the Industrials, Utilities, and Technology sectors leading Friday’s declines.


## 🟢 Leaders

- **ESTC** **+20.3%**

- **GAP** **+14.3%**

- **AFRM** **+10.2%**

- **AMZN** **+4.02%**

- **CRM** **+3.06%**


## 🔴 Laggards

- **PYPL** **-12.71%**

- **MRVL** **-10.28%**

- **CRWD** **-6.4%**

- **NVDA** **-4.57%**

- **MMM** **-2.56%**


## Earnings

- 🟢 Elastic ( **ESTC**) surged **+20.3%** to roughly **$100**, a new 2026 high, after fiscal Q1 revenue of **$478M** and EPS of **$0.70** beat estimates and the company lifted full-year guidance to **$3.29-$3.37** per share.

- 🟢 Gap ( **GAP**) beat on EPS ( **$0.57** vs. **$0.55** est.) on **10%** comparable-sales growth at the flagship Gap brand, and named retail veteran Michael Francis as the new CEO of its struggling Old Navy unit. Shares jumped **+14.3%** even as Old Navy comps fell **-4%** and the company trimmed its full-year sales-growth outlook.

- 🟢 Affirm ( **AFRM**) jumped **+10.2%** after fiscal Q4 revenue of **$1.17B** topped the **$1.11B** estimate, with first-quarter guidance also above expectations.

- 🔴 **NVDA** posted fiscal second-quarter revenue of **$96.22B**, up **106%** year-over-year and roughly **5%** above estimates, with EPS of **$2.22** beating the **$2.09** consensus; management guided to **70%** revenue growth for fiscal 2028. Shares still fell **-4.57%** to **$217.55**, as the print — while blowout — wasn’t enough to reignite Thursday’s broader chip rally.

- 🔴 CrowdStrike ( **CRWD**) slipped **-6.4%**, giving back some of its post-earnings surge from earlier in the week on routine profit-taking.

- 🔴 Marvell ( **MRVL**) beat on both lines, with fiscal Q2 revenue of **$2.74B** ( **+37%** YoY) and non-GAAP EPS of **$0.94** versus **$0.93** expected, and raised its FY2027 and FY2028 revenue guidance to **$12B** and **$18B**. Shares still fell **-10.28%** to **$216.62** as investors focused on softer gross-margin guidance and a lack of near-term detail on the timing of its Google partnership revenue.


## AI

- 🔴 **NVDA**‘s blowout quarter reassured investors that AI demand remains intact, but shares still fell **-4.57%** (see Earnings) as the broader semiconductor complex couldn’t extend Thursday’s rally into Friday, underscoring how sensitive the AI trade remains to any ambiguity in the details.

- 🔴 **MRVL**‘s **-10.28%** post-earnings drop (see Earnings) reflected investor impatience over the pace at which its Google partnership converts to revenue — a dynamic worth watching into Broadcom ( **AVGO**)’s own AI-chip report next week (see Tomorrow’s Calendar).

- 🟡 **NVDA** (see Corporate) reportedly agreed to acquire AI model hub Hugging Face for **$12.9B**, a move toward controlling more of the AI software stack even as “circular financing” concerns among AI infrastructure spenders continue to linger in the background.


## Corporate

- 🟢 Amazon ( **AMZN**) rallied **+4.02%** (see Leaders) after Evercore lifted its price target to **$355**, citing strong retail signals.

- 🟡 **NVDA** (-4.57%, see Earnings) reportedly agreed to acquire Hugging Face, the open-source AI model repository, for **$12.9B**.

- 🔴 **PYPL** tumbled **-12.71%** to **$53.66** after Bloomberg reported that a buyout consortium led by Stripe and private-equity firm Advent International — which had offered roughly **$60.50** a share (about **$53B**) in mid-July — abandoned its pursuit after the two sides failed to agree on price.


## Market Structure

- 🟡 No S&P 500, Dow, or Nasdaq-100 index changes or market-structure rule changes were announced for today’s session.


## Macro/Policy

- 🔴 Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivered his first Jackson Hole keynote, saying the central bank “will have work to do” if officials aren’t confident inflation is returning to the **2%** target, and that recent CPI and PCE readings — while better than feared — don’t yet show meaningful underlying improvement.

- 🔴 Fed funds futures repriced sharply hawkish on the remarks: odds of a September rate hike jumped to roughly **57%**, up from about **35%** heading into the speech.


## Treasury Bonds

- 🔴 **2-year** yield jumped roughly **12bps** on the day to **4.36%**, the sharpest short-end move in more than two months, as traders priced in higher hike odds.

- 🔴 **10-year** yield rose about **5-6bps** to **4.72%**.

- 🔴 **30-year** yield edged up **2bps** to **5.21%**.

- 🔴 The **2s10s spread** narrowed to roughly **36bps** from **44bps** ahead of the speech, as the front end repriced faster than the long end.


## Geopolitics

- 🟡 The Strait of Hormuz blockade tied to the ongoing US-Iran conflict remained in the background — Iran’s foreign trade has reportedly plunged **35%** under the US blockade — but wasn’t a primary driver of Friday’s session, with **WTI crude** little changed on the day (see Commodities).


## Foreign Markets

- 🟢 **Europe’s STOXX 600** advanced **+0.5%**, absorbing the hawkish Warsh commentary with relative calm.

- 🟢 **Japan’s Nikkei 225** climbed **+0.41%** to **66,405.56**, extending its post-Nvidia-earnings tech bid.

- 🟡 **Hong Kong’s Hang Seng** was roughly flat, up **+0.07%** to **25,584.79**.

- 🔴 **Mainland China’s Shanghai Composite** slipped **-0.11%** to **3,952.18**.


## Currencies

- 🟢 **DXY** rose **+0.5%** to **99.65**, reclaiming its 200-day moving average near **99.17** and approaching its 100-day average near **99.60** as the hawkish Fed repricing lifted the dollar broadly.

- 🟢 **USD/JPY** rose **+0.42%** to **159.97**.

- 🟢 **GBP/USD** fell **-0.43%** to **1.3531**, its weakest since **August 19**.

- 🟢 **EUR/USD** fell **-0.57%** to **1.1583**, its weakest since **August 19**.


## Commodities

- 🟡 **WTI crude** (October contract) was little changed, down **-0.17%** to **$83.39**, with the ongoing Hormuz blockade (see Geopolitics) still underpinning a persistent risk premium.

- 🔴 **Gold** plunged **-3.41%** to **$4,504.80** — a notably outsized move relative to its typical daily range — as the hawkish Warsh remarks drove real yields and the dollar higher, pressuring the non-yielding metal off its recent three-month high near **$4,700**.


## Crypto

- 🔴 Bitcoin ( **BTC**) fell **-3.14%** to **$77,598.69**, tracking the broader risk-off tone after Warsh’s hawkish remarks and pulling back from a three-month high near **$81,455** earlier in the week.

- 🟡 Spot Bitcoin ETFs saw roughly **$201.9M** in outflows on the day, ending a nine-session inflow streak that had brought in about **$3.04B**; Ethereum and Solana-linked products continued to see inflows.


## Prediction Markets

- 🟡 Fed rate-hike odds for September (see Macro/Policy) repriced sharply on prediction markets and futures alike following the Warsh speech.

- 🟡 A same-day S&P 500 directional contract on Lines.com resolved **NO** (down close), with total volume of roughly **$79,434** — the contract had opened near **52%** implied probability for an up close, reflecting genuine two-way uncertainty ahead of the speech.


## Volatility

- 🟢 **VIX** closed at **14.46**, down **-0.34%**, staying historically subdued even as the rate-hike repricing intensified — a sign vol markets read the move as a policy-path shift rather than a new shock.

- 🟡 Front-end vol should stay in focus into next week’s heavier catalyst slate (see Tomorrow’s Calendar).


## Tomorrow & Next Week’s Calendar

- **Monday, 8/31**: Quiet on the U.S. data front. Before the bell: Science Applications International ( **SAIC**).

- **Tuesday, 9/1**: **ISM Manufacturing PMI** (10:00 AM ET), **July JOLTS** job openings (10:00 AM ET). After the close: Palo Alto Networks ( **PANW**), Dell Technologies ( **DELL**).

- **Wednesday, 9/2**: **ADP employment report** (8:15 AM ET), Fed **Beige Book** release. After the close: **AVGO**, Hewlett Packard Enterprise ( **HPE**), NetApp ( **NTAP**), Snowflake ( **SNOW**).

- **Friday, 9/4**: **August jobs report** — nonfarm payrolls and unemployment rate — the week’s headline release ahead of the Fed’s September 15-16 meeting.


## 3 Scenarios

- 🟢 Bullish: **AVGO**‘s AI-chip print beats and raises Wednesday, the August jobs report comes in soft enough to cool hike bets without spooking growth fears, and equities reclaim this week’s highs into the long weekend.

- 🟡 Neutral: Earnings stay a stock-by-stock story (per this week’s beat-but-sell-off pattern), the jobs report lands close to expectations, and indices chop in a tight range as the market waits on the September FOMC.

- 🔴 Bearish: A hot jobs report cements September hike odds near certainty, **AVGO** disappoints on AI-chip guidance, and the dollar/yield move that hit gold and small-caps Friday extends into a broader risk-off week.


## Final Take

Friday’s session was really about one thing: **Fed Chair Warsh using his first Jackson Hole speech to tell markets the inflation fight isn’t over.**

That single message pushed short-end yields up the most in two months, lifted the dollar, and helped drive an outsized drop in gold — even as it barely dented the major indices, which still closed out a winning week.

Underneath the headline number, the real story was a market punishing any imperfection in earnings: **NVDA** and **MRVL** both beat and still fell, while **ESTC**, **GAP**, and **AFRM** all rallied double digits on clean beats.

**PYPL**‘s collapse after its buyout fell through was the day’s cleanest single-stock casualty, a reminder that deal premium can vanish as fast as it built.

Heading into next week, the market has two clear tells: whether **AVGO** can deliver an AI print clean enough to avoid the sell-the-news treatment, and whether Friday’s jobs report validates or unwinds the sharp repricing in rate-hike odds.

Source: CNBC, Yahoo Finance, Reuters, Bloomberg, Trading Economics, The Motley Fool, TheStreet, Investrade.

, Reuters -

\\* Friday's monthly employment data expected to show
58,000-job increase

\\* Broadcom( AVGO ) earnings highlight last batch of results for
strong Q2 season

\\* Manufacturing, services reports also to shed light on
economy's health

By Lewis Krauskopf

NEW YORK, Aug 28 (Reuters) - A fresh look at the U.S. labor
market in the coming week along with quarterly results from
semiconductor company Broadcom( AVGO ) will test a market rally
that has lifted stocks near record highs.
The S&P 500 posted a weekly gain, putting the benchmark
index slightly more than 1% away from its August 13 all-time
high. A blowout quarterly report on Wednesday from AI bellwether
and market behemoth Nvidia( NVDA ) boosted sentiment for
stocks, which had been dented earlier in the month by rising
Treasury yields.

Investors were focused on the monthly U.S. employment
report, due on September 4, and on whether the jobs data would
offer hints about the U.S. Federal Reserve's plans for interest
rates in coming months.

"As we're starting to get closer to that September (Fed)
meeting, each data print is going to be under the microscope as
it may inform what the Fed ultimately does," said Michael
Reynolds, vice president of investment strategy at Glenmede.
Following a speech by new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh on Friday,
investors increased bets that the central bank would hike rates
at its next meeting in September, as it grapples with
above-target inflation.

AUGUST JOBS DATA IN FOCUS
With August coming to a close, the S&P 500 was last up more than
12% for the year. Strong corporate profit growth driven by
massive spending on the AI infrastructure buildout is fueling
the nearly four-year-old bull run in U.S. equities.

Markets have been relatively calm as summer ends in the U.S.
The Cboe Volatility Index hovered near its low point for
the year, and daily market trading volume this week was well
below its 2026 average.

Several upcoming events could shake assets, including the
jobs data. Employment for August was expected to have climbed by
58,000 jobs, with the unemployment rate at 4.1%, according to a
Reuters poll as of Friday.
The July report showed a surprise labor-market weakening, with
employment declining by 23,000 jobs.

"The last jobs report gave the market and investors a little
bit of pause," said Amanda Agati, chief investment officer of
PNC Asset Management Group.

However, Agati said she doubted there was a breakdown in the
labor market, adding she would be looking for "either
confirmation of that trend that we saw in the last report, or
maybe a bounce back to prior months."

RATE PATH IN FOCUS WITH JOBS DATA
The jobs data could also indicate whether the Fed is likely to
raise interest rates. Data this week showed inflation continued
to run well above the U.S. central bank's 2% annual target.

Rate hikes pose several challenges for equity performance,
including by raising borrowing costs for consumers and
companies.

Fed funds futures late on Friday suggested a 57% chance of a
hike at the next meeting in September, and investors were wary
that a hot jobs report showing a big jump in employment and
sharp wage growth could increase such bets.

"What the stock market wants to see is a continued number
that gives the Fed the ability to remain on hold," said Matt
Stucky, chief portfolio manager, equities, at Northwestern
Mutual Wealth Management.
Other economic data in the coming week included reports on
manufacturing and services sector activity. The prior monthly
reading from the Institute for Supply Management showed U.S.
manufacturing activity increased to the highest level in more
than four years.

"Continuing that momentum into September we think is
something that's really noteworthy to watch," Stucky said.

BROADCOM RESULTS DUE AS Q2 SEASON NEARS END

Wednesday's earnings report from Broadcom( AVGO ), whose market
value was last about $1.7 trillion, will also be in focus, after
rival semiconductor company Nvidia's( NVDA ) results lifted equity
indexes.

Nvidia( NVDA ) forecast a whopping 70% jump in revenue for its next
fiscal year. It was a rare disclosure for the AI bellwether,
which typically does not issue such projections.

"We're just wondering whether or not Broadcom( AVGO ) offers the
same type of visibility," Stucky said.

Other reports are due next week from tech companies Dell
Technologies( DELL ) and Palo Alto Networks( PANW ). With the
vast majority of companies having already reported, S&P 500
second-quarter earnings are on pace to have climbed 34.5% from a
year earlier on an adjusted basis, according to LSEG IBES data.
The reporting season has demonstrated "really robust core
earnings power," Reynolds said.

"If we continue to see that with the last few reports in the
next week, I think that's really constructive for what the rest
of the year looks like," Reynolds said.
(Reporting by Lewis Krauskopf in New York; Editing by Colin Barr
and Matthew Lewis)

## 1\. Today's US Market Summary

The US stock market closed lower across all three indices on Friday, August 28. The S&P 500 fell 0.25% from the previous day to 7,711.76, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.02% to 53,559.99, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.52% to 26,402.42. While the decline rates were small, the substance was not merely profit-taking. It was a stock market decline accompanied by rising interest rates, taking the form of a textbook valuation adjustment where the present value of future earnings is eroded through an increase in the discount rate.

## 2\. The path indicated by Chair Warsh at Jackson Hole

The Jackson Hole Economic Symposium is a meeting hosted by the Kansas City Fed every August. It has a history of being used by successive Fed Chairs to signal shifts in policy direction, and the market watches this speech closely every year. The speaker for 2026 was Chair Kevin Warsh.

According to reports, Chair Warsh made clear his stance that returning the inflation rate to the 2% target is the top priority, stating that some improvement in inflation indicators over the summer does not mean that underlying inflation has sufficiently subsided. Central banks are always playing tug-of-war between two mandates: price stability and maximum employment. It is easy when these two are pointing in the same direction, but when prices remain high while employment begins to decline, as is the case in the US now, one must always be prioritized. Chair Warsh's speech indicated that this priority lies on the side of prices.

### The significance of Jackson Hole

I will add a note on why a single speech can move the market so much.

The Jackson Hole Economic Symposium has a different character from the regular press conferences after an FOMC meeting. The post-FOMC press conference is a venue to explain the policy decision just made. The Chair is required to speak within the scope of the decided content and finds it difficult to develop personal views extensively. In contrast, Jackson Hole takes the form of an academic meeting, where the Chair can discuss medium-term policy philosophy and economic views without being bound by immediate decisions.

This difference is important. What the market wants to know is not just 'what will be done at the next meeting,' but the framework itself of 'what kind of organization this central bank is and what it prioritizes.' Jackson Hole is one of the few opportunities where that framework is discussed, which is why the market pays close attention to this speech at the end of August every year.

And this time, the market perceived that the framework had changed. It is more natural to think that the move in the September rate hike probability from 35% to 57% was not because the forecast for the single September meeting changed, but because the understanding of the Fed's reaction function itself was updated. A reaction function is the correspondence relationship where the central bank reacts in a certain way if economic indicators move in a certain way. Until now, the market had assumed a reaction function of 'moving toward easing if the economy slows down.' Chair Warsh's speech implied a different reaction function: 'as long as inflation is above the target, the central bank will not ease based on economic slowdown alone.'

An update to the reaction function affects a much wider range than an update to a single forecast. This is because not only September, but also October, December, and next year's outlook are all rewritten at the same time. That is why the 2-year Treasury yield moved by as much as 12 basis points.

### What a flattening yield curve signifies

Here, we will delve a bit deeper into the relationship between 2-year and 10-year bonds. A basis point is 0.01%, and in the world of interest rates, we discuss them in units where 1% is divided into 100 parts. On August 28, 2-year bonds rose by over 12 basis points, while 10-year bonds rose by about 5.6 basis points. This means that, net, the short-term rates moved significantly more by over 6 basis points.

A yield curve is a graph with the remaining maturity on the horizontal axis and the yield on the vertical axis. It is usually upward-sloping. This is because the longer money is lent, the higher the risk, so a higher yield is required. When the slope of this curve becomes gentler, it is called flattening.

There are two typical situations where flattening occurs. One is a phase where the central bank is tightening monetary policy. While short-term interest rates, which are strongly influenced by policy rates, rise, long-term interest rates reflect future average economic growth and inflation rates, so they are less likely to rise if tightening is expected to suppress future growth. The other is a phase where an economic recession is approaching. In this case, the curve inverts, resulting in a state called an inverted yield curve where short-term interest rates exceed long-term interest rates.

The US is currently in the first situation. The market views it as, 'The FRB will tighten from here on, but because that will slow down the economy, the average interest rate level 10 years from now will not rise that much.' In other words, the bond market interprets the current expectations for rate hikes as 'a policy that sacrifices the economy to fight inflation.'

This interpretation is doubly harsh for the stock market. Rising interest rates push down valuations, and an economic slowdown pushes down corporate earnings themselves. It is a structure where both the numerator and denominator are deteriorating, and the background to the Nasdaq Composite falling 0.52% on August 28 lies in this dual pressure.

### The Yardstick of Real Interest Rates

Another essential concept for interpreting the bond market is the real interest rate. This is the value obtained by subtracting the inflation rate from the nominal interest rate, representing the increase in purchasing power that an investor actually gains after accounting for price increases.

The nominal yield on the US 10-year Treasury note is 4.717%, and the consumer price inflation rate is 3.4%, so the real yield is approximately 1.3 percentage points by simple subtraction. In contrast, Japan's 10-year bond yield is 2.928% minus a CPI of 1.9%, resulting in approximately 1.0 percentage point, while Germany's is 3.273% minus a Eurozone HICP of 2.9%, resulting in approximately 0.4 percentage points.

A level near real zero is evaluated as a state where monetary policy is close to neutral—neither tightening nor easing—or perhaps even slightly leaning toward easing.

The basis for Chair Warsh's stance of not ruling out the possibility of interest rate hikes likely lies in this calculation. As long as the inflation rate remains in the high 3% range, keeping the nominal interest rate at 3.75% is effectively no different from continuing monetary easing.

I will add a supplement regarding the concept of interest rate sensitivity. The theoretical price of a stock is expressed as the sum of future cash flows discounted to present value. When the discount rate rises, the present value falls, but the magnitude of the impact depends on when the cash flow occurs. $100 one year from now discounted at 4% is about $96, but $100 ten years from now discounted at the same 4% is about $68. If the discount rate rises to 5%, it is about $95 one year from now and about $61 ten years from now. While the cash flow one year from now only decreases by about 1 percentage point, the cash flow ten years from now decreases by more than 10 percentage points.

This calculation is the entire reason why growth stocks fall more than utility stocks during periods of rising interest rates. Because growth companies are expected to have the majority of their profits in the distant future, their prices react significantly to changes in the discount rate. The price movement on August 28, where the Dow 30 fell only 0.02% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.52%, can be said to be an observation of this logic.

Therefore, the stronger the expectations for interest rate hikes toward the FOMC in September, the more the performance gap between the indices may widen. Conversely, if the ISM Manufacturing PMI comes in weak and expectations for interest rate hikes recede, the Nasdaq will be the first to be bought back.

## 8\. Medium- to Long-Term Implications

I will organize three points that can be read from this phase.

The first is that the framework of monetary policy is at a turning point. Throughout the first half of the 2020s, the market has operated on the premise that "if inflation settles down, the central bank will shift to easing." Chairman Warsh's speech this time showed that this premise does not automatically hold true. As long as inflation remains high in the 3% range, easing may not come even if the economy slows down. The process of pricing in this possibility will proceed over the next few months.

The second is that supply-side factors are constraining monetary policy. The background to why US inflation is not falling completely is not just the strength of demand, but also the surge in energy prices. With WTI crude oil up 48.15% and gasoline up 102.37% year-to-date, the fact that the Consumer Price Index remains at 3.4% itself can be said to indicate the stability of other items. However, while monetary policy can suppress demand, it cannot restart navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. If inflation persists due to factors that the central bank cannot control, interest rate hikes could end up hurting only the economy without being effective on prices.

The third is the level of real interest rates. The level of 0.35% in real terms, calculated by subtracting 3.4% inflation from a 3.75% nominal rate, is historically accommodative. If the Fed is serious about returning inflation to 2%, the necessary rate hike magnitude might not be satisfied by the single 25-basis-point hike the market has priced in. Conversely, the scenario of one rate hike in September and then stopping is half-baked from the perspective of curbing inflation. What the market has not yet priced in may not be the presence or absence of rate hikes, but the possibility that rate hikes will not end with just one.

How to position yourself as an investment decision depends on your respective time horizon. However, at the very least, the following point is worth keeping in mind. In phases where stocks and bonds fall simultaneously, traditional diversification does not function well. August 28, 2026, was exactly that kind of day. It was a development where rising interest rates pushed down stock valuations while simultaneously lowering bond prices themselves.
